name: Jade Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm usually in my bedroom, which is also my studio, recording violin parts for songwriters who send me files from all over. Afternoons I teach eight kids violin, some at my flat and some at their houses. Most weekends from May to September I play weddings with a string quartet, and in winter it's whatever I can find.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of your money comes from each of those?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Roughly a third each, though the recording third has been shrinking for a year. The quartet pays a hundred and twenty a wedding, and a remote string part pays between fifty and a hundred and fifty. I share a flat with my friend Priya, who's a barista, and we both check the bank app more than we'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about paying musicians properly. I'd post something about streaming rates, because that was the problem before AI and it's still the problem. At the quartet we'd joke about it between sets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, even the routine stuff touches me. The apps that clean up and tune a string part already mean songwriters ask for one take instead of three. Even if AI stays a gimmick, my remote recording work has dropped by a third this year, and a gimmick is enough to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push harder on the weddings: a proper website, and asking the venues on the coast road to list us. I'd look for two more violin pupils. And I'd keep using the transcription app to write out parts, because it saves me an evening a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Low-level worried, like always. Not frightened, just tired of being one cancelled wedding away from a bad month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one cancelled wedding. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In June a couple called it off two weeks before, and we only had a fifty-pound deposit each. That month I paid rent late for the first time and Priya didn't say anything, which was worse. Now we ask for a bigger deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for how things are, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The streaming companies, mostly, and the labels that signed deals on our behalf. A song can get a million plays and the session players see nothing. I don't blame the couples or the songwriters; they're broke too.

say: Now can we talk about **paying musicians** properly, instead of AI hype.
**Streaming rates** were the problem before AI, and they still are.
think: My **remote recording** work has already dropped by a third this year.
Tuning apps mean songwriters ask for **one take** instead of three.
do: Build a **wedding website** and get listed with venues on the coast road.
Find **two more** violin pupils before winter.
Keep using the **transcription app** to save an evening a week.
feel: **Low-level worried**, and **tired** of being one cancelled wedding from a bad month.
S0.quote: Even if AI stays a gimmick, my remote recording work has dropped by a third this year, and a gimmick is enough to do that.
fieldNote: Even in **AI Plateau** her recording income is already **shrinking**.
A **cancelled wedding** in June made her pay rent late for the first time.

steps.text: Build a quartet website and ask coast-road venues to list it

Use the transcription app to write out string parts each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who made these tools trained them on our recordings and never paid us a penny. I'd share the union's campaign for consent and payment, and I'd go to the meeting in the city. At weddings I'd say it plainly to the planners: live players or nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the recording third of my income is gone. A songwriter can type "warm string quartet, sad" and get something good enough. I'll still have weddings and pupils, but losing a third of my income on under a month of savings means I can't make rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop chasing remote sessions within a few months and put that time into teaching, maybe a small group string class at the library on Saturdays. I'd try the AI booking tools other quartets use, once I saw they actually worked. And I'd pick up café shifts with Priya over winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gutted, but not surprised. I've sort of watched this one coming for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the tools once they worked. How do you square that with being angry about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't fully. I'm angry about how they were made, not about using a calendar that books itself. If the other quartets use it to get more weddings and I don't, I'm just losing twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The new bow I've been saving towards, about six hundred. Then the summer course in Vienna I wanted to do. Food and rent stay, and my phone stays because pupils book through it.

fieldNote: She separates anger at how AI was **made** from **using** practical tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and public money for the arts, and we needed them yesterday. I'd be on every march. Online I'd post about a guaranteed income, because I can't see what else would work in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years means the recording work goes, and probably the online teaching apps eat into the rest. Weddings would last a bit longer because people want real faces at a wedding. By the time the robots arrive in 2031, I'd already have been living on wedding money and café shifts for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full-time at the café, or anything with a regular wage, straight away, and keep the quartet for weekends. I'd join the union's emergency fund and apply for any arts grant going. If rent went up, I'd move back in with my parents in the valley, which is an hour from any venue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, and a little bit numb. I think I'd stop practising for a while, which has never happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said thinking AI comes first and robots later. Which parts of your work buy you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The playing in a room, and teaching little ones to hold a violin without a squeaky mess. A screen can explain a scale, but it can't move a seven-year-old's elbow. So I'd get those three years, but only if parents can still afford lessons, and in that world I doubt they could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm not giving up, I'm pausing. My dad drives a delivery van, so he'd be scared for his own job too. I'd probably end up helping him more than he helps me.

say: We need **unions** and **public arts money**, and we needed them yesterday.
A **guaranteed income** is the only thing I can see working in two years.
think: Recording work goes and **online lessons** eat the rest within two years.
By **2031** I'd have lived on wedding money and café shifts for three years.

fieldNote: Hands-on teaching of **small children** is the part she thinks lasts longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up proper rules: consent for training data, a share for musicians, public funding for live music. I'd help write the union's letter to our local representative. At weddings I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years is enough to make a plan, which is more than I've ever had. The remote recording goes in the first year or two whatever happens. With five years I could become the violin teacher every parent in town knows, and a machine won't take a seven-year-old's elbow and fix it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train in a method for teaching very young children; the courses run on weekends and cost about eight hundred over a year. I'd use AI tools for scheduling and invoices, the boring bits, once I've seen another teacher do it. And I'd try to save a hundred a month from the wedding season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but awake. There's a plan in it, and that helps more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does eight hundred come from, with your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Spread over a year it's about sixty-five a month, which is roughly what I spend on takeaways and the bus. I'd cycle to pupils and cook with Priya. My gran also said she'd help with courses, and for once I'd say yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cellist in our quartet, Mira. She only does recording and weddings, she doesn't teach, and she isn't keen on kids. I'd try to get her into the group classes anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have ten years, so there's no excuse. Fund music in schools, pay players fairly, make AI companies pay for what they trained on. I'd keep saying it at union meetings, in a calmer voice than in the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven. I'd have time to build a teaching practice and maybe a family. My worry with ten years is that I'd get comfortable, and then wake up at thirty-five with the same rent and no plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same plan as the five-year one, just slower and saner. I'd do the early-years teaching course within two years, then look for a part-time post at a music school. I'd ask Priya if she wants to share a bigger flat with a room I could teach in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Like there's air in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the robots arriving around 2039 change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in the next ten years, because my work is mostly bows and fingers and kids. By 2039 I'd hope to be the teacher parents trust, and a robot doesn't win that in a day. But I'm guessing; I don't know how good they'll be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a family. Would this change those plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boyfriend Sam and I have talked vaguely about kids around thirty. With ten years, I think we'd still try. With two, I'd have said no straight away.

say: Ten years means there's **no excuse** for not funding music and paying players.
**AI companies** should pay for the recordings they trained on.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven**, with time for a teaching practice and family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough time to change anything, and I'd be serving coffee to the people who built it. What would help is a guaranteed basic income, and AI companies paying musicians for the recordings they trained on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who the music is for. People don't hire a string quartet for the notes; they hire us so their grandmother cries in the right place. I'd like that written down somewhere.

headlineQuote: People don't hire a string quartet for the notes; they hire us so their grandmother cries in the right place.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old violinist** who records remote parts, plays wedding quartets and teaches eight children.
She shares a flat with Priya, a barista, and has **under a month** saved.
She blames **streaming companies** and AI firms that trained on musicians without paying.
She uses **AI tools** for chores once proven, while campaigning with the **union**.
Her plan in the slower scenarios is to become a trusted **early-years teacher**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to change anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income**, and AI companies **paying musicians** for what they trained on.
